evidence: src/application/dtos.ts declares only the use-case contracts (CreateUserInput, CreateProjectInput, CreateTaskInput, TaskFilterInput, UserDto, ProjectDto, TaskDto), and all of them are used by TaskManagementService.

src/application/task-management-service.ts: TaskManagementService's constructor injects UserRepository, ProjectRepository, TaskRepository and IdGenerator, and every method goes through these interfaces.
src/application/task-management-service.ts: the private requireProject(id) keeps the project-existence check in one place, shared by createTask and listProjectTasks.
src/application/task-management-service.ts: the private toTaskDto(task) is the only place a Task becomes a TaskDto, used by createTask, listProjectTasks and markTaskDone.
src/application/task-management-service.ts: markTaskDone calls the domain method task.markDone() instead of setting status itself, so the domain's own logic is used.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: This module passes. Both files deal with one concern: the application-layer use cases for managing users, projects and tasks. dtos.ts defines the input and output contracts. task-management-service.ts is the only service, and it uses those contracts for every public method. The service goes through its abstractions as intended. It reaches persistence and ID generation only through the injected interfaces (UserRepository, ProjectRepository, TaskRepository, IdGenerator). It builds domain entities and calls entity behaviour (task.markDone()) rather than editing status directly. Each rule lives in one place. The project-existence check is in the private requireProject method, used by both createTask and listProjectTasks. Turning a Task into a TaskDto is done only in toTaskDto, and the due-date parse-and-validate check happens only once, in createTask. One small inconsistency: the user and project DTOs are built inline, while tasks use a helper. Each of those inline mappings happens only once, so nothing is duplicated and it doesn't count as a violation.
